# NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect

Pratibha Zunjare Affiliation: Electrical and Computer Engineering  
Virginia Tech  
Blacksburg, USA  
pratibhaz@vt.edu    Michael S. Hsiao Affiliation: Electrical and
Computer Engineering  
Virginia Tech  
Blacksburg, USA  
hsiao@vt.edu

###### Abstract

We present NeuroProlog, a neurosymbolic framework that compiles math
word problems into executable Prolog programs and trains LLMs to
internalize symbolic structure rather than apply it post-hoc. Our
multi-task Cocktail objective jointly supervises formula-to-rule
translation (KB) and natural language-to-program synthesis (SOLVE)
within a shared symbolic space, combining declarative knowledge with
procedural reasoning supervision improves compositional reasoning. At
inference, an execution-guided decoding pipeline with a five-class error
taxonomy enables zero-shot iterative program repair without
correction-specific training.

On GSM8K across four model scales (3B–32B), Cocktail FT yields
statistically significant gains for three of four models: +5.23% for
Qwen-32B, +3.43% for GPT-OSS-20B, and +5.54% for Llama-3B; GPT-OSS-20B
Cocktail FT achieves the highest accuracy among the evaluated
configurations at 88.34%. Error analysis reveals scale-associated
differences in failure and repair behavior across the evaluated models.
These results demonstrate the potential of combining symbolic knowledge
and execution feedback to improve LLM-based mathematical reasoning.

###### Index Terms: 

Large Language Models, Neurosymbolic AI, Mathematical Reasoning,
Multi-Task Learning

## I Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on
mathematical reasoning benchmarks such as GSM8K \[[1](#bib.bib1)\],
aided by techniques like Chain-of-Thought prompting \[[2](#bib.bib2)\]
and Program-of-Thoughts \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]. However, recent studies
reveal that LLM reasoning often relies on probabilistic pattern matching
rather than formal logical inference \[[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5)\].
This leads to brittle behavior: models produce plausible but incorrect
solutions, fail under perturbations, and cannot verify intermediate
reasoning steps \[[6](#bib.bib6)\].

Neurosymbolic approaches attempt to address these limitations by
integrating neural models with symbolic representations or external
solvers, combining neural flexibility with symbolic
rigor \[[6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7), [8](#bib.bib8)\]. However,
existing methods typically apply symbolic reasoning as a post-hoc
correction mechanism at inference time—validating or refining LLM
outputs using external theorem provers or logic
engines \[[9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10)\]. This decoupled design
prevents models from internalizing symbolic structure during training:
the symbolic components serve as verification tools rather than learned
reasoning capabilities. Consequently, LLMs remain weak at systematic
generalization to novel problem compositions and struggle to produce
verifiable, executable reasoning traces without external intervention.

Grounded mathematical reasoning, we posit, requires models to jointly
learn three core capabilities: (i) mapping natural language to formal
logic, (ii) generating executable programs that encode structured
reasoning, and (iii) aligning symbolic outputs with numeric
verification. To address this gap, we present NeuroProlog, a unified
neurosymbolic framework that enforces formal reasoning through
multi-task _Cocktail_ training \[[11](#bib.bib30)\] as shown in
Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Fig. 1 ‣ I Introduction ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect").
Our approach supervises LLMs on formula translation, program synthesis,
and execution verification simultaneously within a shared symbolic
representation space, inducing cross-task transfer and enabling models
to internalize systematic reasoning patterns rather than relying on
superficial heuristics.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 1: Comparison of traditional LLM fine-tuning with NeuroProlog.

We construct a multi-task dataset combining symbolic mathematical
knowledge and word problems with executable program traces. Symbolic
structure paired with semantic alignment guides the model to generate
interpretable, verifiable outputs. At inference, an execution-guided
decoding pipeline provides iterative feedback to correct program errors,
measuring not only final accuracy but also the model’s ability to
recover from logical mistakes. The main contributions of this work are
as follows:

- •
  Multi-Task Neurosymbolic Training: A Cocktail objective combining
  declarative knowledge (formula-to-Prolog) with procedural
  problem-solving (word-problem-to-program), inducing cross-task
  transfer within a unified symbolic representation space.
- •
  Execution-Guided Decoding: An iterative refinement pipeline with a
  5-class error taxonomy enabling zero-shot execution-guided program
  repair without correction-specific training.
- •
  Scale-Dependent Error Shift: Empirical discovery that Cocktail
  training qualitatively transforms error distributions at large scale
  (TYPE_ERROR $`\rightarrow`$ DOMAIN_ERROR at 32B) but not at small
  scale (SYNTAX $`\rightarrow`$ TYPE at 8B), revealing a capacity
  threshold ($`\sim`$10B parameters) for semantic type understanding.
- •
  Comprehensive Evaluation: Rigorous experiments across 12
  configurations (4 models $`\times`$ 3 settings) demonstrating
  statistically significant gains (+3.43% to +5.54%, $`p{<}0.05`$) for 3
  of 4 models, with strongest performance (88.34%) exceeding all
  comparable baselines.
- •
  Open Release: Complete dataset (200 KB entries + 310 SOLVE problems +
  7476 updated GSM8K-Prolog problems), training code, evaluation
  pipeline, and LoRA adapters for all 8 fine-tuned configurations.

## II Related Work

Mathematical Reasoning in LLMs. Recent LLMs achieve strong performance
on mathematical benchmarks through intermediate reasoning techniques.
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting \[[2](#bib.bib2)\] generates natural
language rationales with extensions including zero-shot
CoT \[[12](#bib.bib11)\] and self-consistency
decoding \[[13](#bib.bib12)\]. Program-Aided Language Models
(PAL) \[[14](#bib.bib13)\] and Program-of-Thoughts
(PoT) \[[3](#bib.bib3)\] delegate computation to Python interpreters,
generating executable code as reasoning traces. However, these
approaches operate at inference time through prompting rather than
internalizing symbolic reasoning during training. Studies show LLMs
perform probabilistic pattern matching rather than systematic
reasoning \[[4](#bib.bib4), [5](#bib.bib5)\], failing under distribution
shifts \[[15](#bib.bib14)\]. We address this through symbolic
supervision during fine-tuning, teaching models to generate verifiable
logical programs.

Neurosymbolic AI. Neurosymbolic approaches combine neural learning with
symbolic logic \[[16](#bib.bib15), [17](#bib.bib16)\].
Logic-LM \[[9](#bib.bib9)\] uses external Prolog solvers, Faithful
CoT \[[18](#bib.bib17)\] translates reasoning to formal logic for
verification, and LINC \[[10](#bib.bib10)\] learns neural-symbolic
translations through self-supervised refinement.
ProSLM \[[19](#bib.bib18)\] integrates Prolog with language models for
explainable, domain-specific question answering. These methods apply
symbolic reasoning post-hoc at inference time. Prolog’s declarative
semantics suit mathematical reasoning, and GSM8K-Prolog provides Prolog
annotations for GSM8K with single-task supervision. We extend this
through multi-task Cocktail training with semantic alignment,
internalizing symbolic structure during training and enabling
self-debugging through execution feedback.

Multi-Task Learning. Multi-task learning improves generalization through
shared representations \[[20](#bib.bib19)\]. The Cocktail
effect \[[21](#bib.bib20)\] produces synergistic gains from
complementary tasks. FLAN \[[22](#bib.bib21)\] and
T0 \[[23](#bib.bib22)\] mix instruction formats, while
CodeT5+ \[[24](#bib.bib23)\] jointly trains on code understanding and
generation. Our Cocktail dataset uniquely combines three supervision
signals: (i) formula-to-Prolog translation for symbolic grounding, (ii)
natural language comments for semantic alignment, and (iii) program
execution for numeric verification, mixing reasoning modalities rather
than task formats.

Program Synthesis and Error Correction. Neural program synthesis methods
include Codex \[[25](#bib.bib24)\], AlphaCode \[[26](#bib.bib25)\], and
CodeLlama \[[27](#bib.bib26)\]. Self-Repair \[[28](#bib.bib27)\] trains
on error-correction pairs, while Reflexion \[[29](#bib.bib28)\] uses
verbal feedback for iterative improvement. These methods target
general-purpose programming rather than formal reasoning. We extend
execution-guided decoding by leveraging Prolog’s error taxonomy to guide
systematic self-correction.

Gaps in Prior Work.
Table [I](#S2.T1 "TABLE I ‣ II Related Work ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")
situates NeuroProlog along five dimensions that collectively define the
design space of neurosymbolic mathematical reasoning systems.

[TABLE]

No prior work jointly trains on formula-to-KB translation or quantifies

Section [IV-G](#S4.SS7 "IV-G Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect").

## III Methodology

We present NeuroProlog, a neurosymbolic framework that enforces
executable mathematical reasoning through multi-task fine-tuning with
Prolog-based symbolic supervision. Our approach consists of three core
components: (1) a unified training corpus combining declarative
mathematical knowledge with procedural problem-solving demonstrations
(Section [III-A](#S3.SS1 "III-A Dataset Construction ‣ III Methodology ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")),
(2) a multi-task Cocktail training objective that induces cross-task
transfer through shared symbolic representations
(Section [III-B](#S3.SS2 "III-B Multi-Task Cocktail Training ‣ III Methodology ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")),
and (3) an execution-guided decoding pipeline with iterative error
feedback
(Section [III-C](#S3.SS3 "III-C Execution-Guided Decoding with Error Feedback ‣ III Methodology ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")).

### III-A Dataset Construction

We construct a unified training corpus designed to enable neurosymbolic
mathematical reasoning through Prolog-based representations. Our dataset
comprises two complementary components: a Mathematical Knowledge Base
(KB) providing declarative symbolic grounding, and a Problem-Solving
Dataset demonstrating procedural application of mathematical concepts.

#### Mathematical Knowledge Base

The KB comprises 200 carefully constructed entries formalizing
fundamental mathematical concepts as executable Prolog predicates. Each
entry follows a standardized instruction-input-output format:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Domain Coverage. The KB entries span 11+ mathematical domains: Basic
Statistics (22 entries, 11.0%), Ratio & Proportion (17, 8.5%),
Percentage Calculations (17, 8.5%), Number Theory (11, 5.5%),
Propositional Logic (9, 4.5%), Boolean Operations (7, 3.5%), Geometry
(12, 6.0%), Linear Equations (6, 3.0%), Sequences & Series (3, 1.5%),
and mixed topics (96, 48.0%).

Semantic Alignment Through Comments. A critical design choice
distinguishes our KB from conventional code datasets: every Prolog
predicate includes natural language comments that explain its
mathematical semantics, enabling the model to bridge informal and formal
reasoning.

#### Problem-Solving Dataset

The second component consists of 310 problem-solving examples based on
the KB, together with 7476 entries from
GSM8K-Prolog \[[30](#bib.bib29)\] with executable Prolog programs:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Quality Assurance. Each entry underwent multi-stage validation: (1)
syntactic verification via SWI-Prolog parsing; (2) execution testing of
each solve/1 predicate; (3) semantic review by domain experts and
researchers.

### III-B Multi-Task Cocktail Training

We formulate neurosymbolic mathematical reasoning as a multi-task
learning problem where models jointly acquire complementary capabilities
through shared symbolic representations.

Task Formulation. Let
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{KB}}=\{(x_{i}^{\text{kb}},y_{i}^{\text{kb}})\}_{i=1}^{200}`$
denote the Knowledge Base dataset, where $`x_{i}^{\text{kb}}`$ is a
natural language description and $`y_{i}^{\text{kb}}`$ is its Prolog
implementation. Let
$`\mathcal{D}_{\text{SOLVE}}=\{(x_{j}^{\text{solve}},y_{j}^{\text{solve}})\}_{j=1}^{7786}`$
denote the Problem-Solving dataset, where $`x_{j}^{\text{solve}}`$ is a
word problem and $`y_{j}^{\text{solve}}`$ is its executable Prolog
program. We train $`f_{\theta}`$ to minimize:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\mathcal{L}_{\text{cocktail}}(\theta)=\lambda_{\text{kb}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{KB}}(\theta)+\lambda_{\text{solve}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{SOLVE}}(\theta),
``` |  | (1) |

with each task-specific loss being the standard causal language modeling
objective:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{KB}}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{KB}}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\right],`$ |  | (2) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{SOLVE}}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal{D}_{\text{SOLVE}}}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}\log p_{\theta}(y_{t}\mid x,y_{<t})\right].`$ |  | (3) |

Task weights satisfy $`\lambda_{\text{kb}}+\lambda_{\text{solve}}=1`$.
Verified answers $`a_{j}`$ are used only during evaluation to identify
logically incorrect executable programs; they are not used during
training.

Training Protocol. We fine-tune using LoRA (without quantization),
injecting low-rank adapters into attention layers while freezing
pretrained weights. Both KB and SOLVE entries are formatted with
task-type prefixes (\[KNOWLEDGE\] vs. \[SOLVE\]) to enable
task-conditional generation. All models share a common optimization
setup (3 epochs, cosine learning rate schedule with 8% warmup, gradient
clipping at 1.0, bfloat16 precision). LoRA rank, learning rate, and
regularization are tuned per model scale, with gradient accumulation
yielding effective batch sizes of 32–64.

Cocktail Effect Hypothesis. The Cocktail effect \[[11](#bib.bib30)\]
suggests complementary multi-task training yields synergistic gains. We
hypothesize three transfer mechanisms: (1) Compositional Reuse (KB
$`\rightarrow`$ SOLVE): KB predicates become reusable building blocks
for SOLVE programs; (2) Contextual Grounding (SOLVE $`\rightarrow`$ KB):
problem-solving provides usage patterns reinforcing abstract formula
semantics; (3) Unified Type System: joint training on Prolog syntax and
CLP(Q) constraints induces shared type-safe representations.

### III-C Execution-Guided Decoding with Error Feedback

At inference time, we introduce an iterative pipeline that leverages
Prolog’s error diagnostics to enable self-debugging through
execution-aware generation.

#### III-C1 Pipeline Architecture

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Fig. 2: NeuroProlog execution-guided decoding pipeline with error
feedback.

Fig. [2](#S3.F2 "Fig. 2 ‣ III-C1 Pipeline Architecture ‣ III-C Execution-Guided Decoding with Error Feedback ‣ III Methodology ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")
illustrates our four-phase pipeline. Given math problem $`q`$,
fine-tuned LLM $`f_{\theta}`$ generates initial Prolog program
$`P_{0}`$. The SWI-Prolog interpreter $`\sigma`$ executes $`P_{0}`$,
producing three possible outcomes: (1) Success with correct answer
(terminate); (2) Success with wrong answer (classify as LOGICAL_ERROR);
(3) Error with diagnostic $`e`$ (classify via taxonomy). On failure, we
generate targeted repair prompt $`\mathcal{P}_{e}`$ containing the
original problem, failed program, error type, and fix instructions. The
model produces corrected program
$`P_{i+1}=f_{\theta}(\mathcal{P}_{e})`$, repeating up to $`k=3`$
iterations.

#### III-C2 Error Taxonomy and Repair Strategies

We distinguish five error classes from SWI-Prolog diagnostics: Syntax
(malformed tokens/brackets), Type (arithmetic on non-numeric terms),
Domain (runtime violations such as division by zero or negative
factorial), Instantiation (variables used before binding), and Logical
(WRONG_ANSWER: program executes but $`\sigma(P)=a^{\prime}\neq a^{*}`$).
For each error class, a targeted repair prompt is applied to address the
corresponding diagnostic category, with class-specific diagnostic codes
and prompt templates used to guide the repair process.

### III-D Evaluation Metrics

We measure performance through five complementary metrics: Accuracy
(final correct answers after $`k\leq 3`$ iterations); Executability
(fraction with at least one valid Prolog execution); initial Success
(solved on attempt 1); Correction Rate (fraction of initial failures
eventually repaired); and Average Iterations (mean execution attempts
per problem).

## IV Experiments

We conduct comprehensive evaluation of NeuroProlog across four LLMs
spanning a 10$`\times`$ parameter range (3B–32B).

### IV-A Experimental Setup

Models. We evaluate four models: (i) Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct
(code-specialized), (ii) GPT-OSS-20B (general-purpose), (iii) Qwen3-8B
(mid-scale general), and (iv) Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct (compact
instruction-tuned).

Training Configurations. For each model we compare three settings: Base
(zero-shot), Prolog FT (fine-tuned on GSM8K-Prolog), and Cocktail FT
(fine-tuned on our unified KB+SOLVE dataset per
Eq. [1](#S3.E1 "In III-B Multi-Task Cocktail Training ‣ III Methodology ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")).
Both fine-tuned configurations use identical LoRA hyperparameters and
train for the same number of epochs.

Decoding and Evaluation. We use greedy decoding (temperature$`=0`$) for
deterministic results. The pipeline runs with $`k{=}3`$ maximum
correction iterations on the full GSM8K test set ($`n{=}1{,}319`$).
Significance is assessed via McNemar’s test.

Cocktail training yields significant gains for three of four models. As
shown in
Fig. [3](#S4.F3 "Fig. 3 ‣ IV-B Overall Performance ‣ IV Experiments ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect"),
Cocktail training improves accuracy by +5.23% ($`p<0.01`$, Qwen-32B),
+3.43% ($`p<0.01`$, GPT-OSS-20B), and +5.54% ($`p<0.05`$, Llama-3B). In
each case, Cocktail FT also outperforms single-task Prolog FT (e.g., by
+2.22% for GPT-OSS). The strongest overall result—88.34% by GPT-OSS-20B
Cocktail FT—demonstrates that multi-task neurosymbolic training can
unlock performance in general-purpose models surpassing larger
code-specialized architectures.

Qwen3-8B reveals a generation–correction trade-off. Qwen3-8B is the only
model where fine-tuning *decreases* accuracy. The base model achieves
66.79% by compensating for poor initial generation (7.7% initial
execution) through strong iterative repair (70.7% correction).
Fine-tuning inverts this profile: initial execution success leaps to
69.8% but correction collapses to 24.1%.

Generalization to MATH-500

To assess out-of-distribution generalization, we evaluate on a
239-problem subset of MATH-500 covering problems with real numeric
answers; problems requiring imaginary numbers, symbolic equation
generation, or geometric constructions are excluded due to SWI-Prolog
CLP(Q) scope. The evaluation protocol is held constant with GSM8K:
identical base models, LoRA hyperparameters, and three-condition
structure (Base, Prolog FT, Cocktail FT). No MATH-500 data was observed
during training.

| Model             | Base  | Cocktail FT | $`\Delta`$ |
|-------------------|-------|-------------|------------|
| Qwen2.5-Coder-32B | 40.17 | 42.68       | +2.51      |
| GPT-OSS-20B       | 49.37 | 51.46       | +2.09      |
| Llama-3B-Instruct | 9.10  | 10.04       | +0.94      |
| Qwen3-8B          | 30.96 | 21.34       | $`-9.62`$  |

TABLE III: Cocktail FT accuracy (%) on MATH-500 subset (239 problems).
$`\Delta`$ denotes change from Base.

The combined KB+SOLVE training configuration improves accuracy over the
corresponding single-task Prolog FT configuration on three of four
models, indicating that incorporating complementary symbolic supervision
can provide additional benefits.

### IV-C Effect of Model Scale

![Refer to caption](2603.02504v3/figures/fig8_scatter_new.jpeg)

Fig. 4: Initial success vs. correction rate across all 12
configurations, revealing four distinct behavioral regimes.

Fig. [4](#S4.F4 "Fig. 4 ‣ IV-C Effect of Model Scale ‣ IV Experiments ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")
plots initial execution success against correction rate for all twelve
configurations, revealing four distinct regimes.

Large code models (32B): Clean generation, emergent correction. Qwen-32B
achieves near-perfect initial success (96.4%) but weak correction
(17.0%). Cocktail training induces a qualitative shift: initial success
decreases to 90.7% while correction improves to 92.7% ($`p<0.01`$).

Medium general models (20B): Error tolerance. GPT-OSS-20B compensates
for moderate initial success (45.0%) with strong correction (81.8%).
Cocktail training shifts toward first-attempt resolution
($`45\%\rightarrow 60\%`$) while maintaining correction quality.

Mid-scale models (8B): Generation–correction trade-off. Qwen3-8B Base
has low initial success (7.7%) but strong correction (70.7%).
Fine-tuning boosts initial success by $`9\times`$ but sharply reduces
correction, lowering overall accuracy ($`p=0.08`$).

Small models (3B): Capacity-limited. Llama-3B-Instruct remains in the
lower-left region regardless of configuration. The 27.07% Cocktail FT
accuracy ceiling confirms 3B parameters are insufficient for reliable
compositional Prolog generation.

### IV-D Execution-Guided Error Recovery

Fig. 5: Final error distribution after $`k{=}3`$ correction attempts, by
Prolog error type.

Cocktail FT trades inital success perfection for robust correction
(Qwen-32B). Cocktail training reduces Qwen-32B’s initial success
accuracy from 96.4% to 90.7% but enables 92.7% error repair, yielding
only 9 final failures versus 39 for the base model (77% reduction).

GPT-OSS-20B: Monotonic pipeline improvement. Fine-tuning monotonically
improves all pipeline metrics: initial success ($`45\%\to 60\%`$),
average iterations ($`1.75\to 1.52`$), and accuracy
($`84.91\%\to 88.34\%`$). The Cocktail configuration requires 13.1%
fewer total iterations than the base while achieving +3.43% higher
accuracy.

Correction degrades at sub-10B scale. Qwen3-8B and Llama-3B-Instruct
exhibit sharp declines in correction rates after fine-tuning
(70.7%$`\rightarrow`$24.1% and 36.2%$`\rightarrow`$8.9%, respectively),
indicating that models below $`\sim`$10B parameters lack sufficient
capacity to jointly learn code generation and execution-based error
diagnosis.

### IV-E Error Analysis

Scale-dependent error shift—the key mechanistic finding. The most
informative result from
Fig. [5](#S4.F5 "Fig. 5 ‣ IV-D Execution-Guided Error Recovery ‣ IV Experiments ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")
is the *opposite* error transformations at different model capacities.
At 32B, base model errors are 87.2% TYPE_ERROR—semantic failures fixable
only 12% of the time. After Cocktail training, errors shift to 55.6%
DOMAIN_ERROR (repaired at 96%). Total errors drop from 39 to 9.

At 8B, the *inverse* occurs: Qwen3-8B base errors are 89.4%
SYNTAX_OPERATOR_EXPECTED. After Cocktail training, the dominant error
becomes 69.5% TYPE_ERROR with only 5% fixability. Fine-tuning
successfully teaches Prolog syntax but *introduces* the same semantic
failure that the 32B model resolves, suggesting semantic type
understanding requires capacity beyond 8B parameters.

### IV-F Pipeline Efficiency

Fig. 6: Accuracy vs. Efficiency tradeoff across all configurations.

We define pipeline efficiency as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\text{Efficiency}=\frac{\text{Accuracy}\times\text{Execution Rate}}{\text{Average Iterations}}.
``` |  | (4) |

Qwen3-8B shows the largest efficiency gain (+61.5%) despite accuracy
loss, as reduced iterations ($`2.43\rightarrow 1.54`$) and improved
executability outweigh accuracy decline for latency-sensitive
applications.
Fig. [6](#S4.F6 "Fig. 6 ‣ IV-F Pipeline Efficiency ‣ IV Experiments ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")
identifies two Pareto-optimal points: GPT-OSS-20B Cocktail for accuracy
(88.34%) and Qwen-32B Prolog FT for efficiency.

### IV-G Ablation Studies

| Model       | Prolog FT | Cocktail FT | $`\Delta`$Acc. | $`\Delta`$Exec. |
|-------------|-----------|-------------|----------------|-----------------|
| Qwen-32B    | 85.14     | 85.52       | +0.38          | +0.08           |
| GPT-OSS-20B | 86.12     | 88.34       | +2.22          | +2.00           |
| Qwen3-8B    | 63.15     | 64.51       | +1.36          | +1.14           |
| Llama-3B    | 21.83     | 27.07       | +5.24          | +15.84          |
| Mean        | 64.06     | 66.36       | +2.30          | +4.77           |

TABLE IV: Effect of Additional Symbolic Supervision

KB Integration.
Table [IV](#S4.T4 "TABLE IV ‣ IV-G Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")
compares the single-task Prolog FT configuration with the combined
KB+SOLVE configuration. The addition of KB supervision improves accuracy
across all four models, with gains ranging from +0.38% to +5.24%.

Execution-Guided Decoding. Taxonomy-based feedback adds +4.82% over
greedy decoding. Qwen-32B Cocktail achieves 90.7% initial success
success, with 92.7% correction rate demonstrating effective
execution-guided repair without correction-specific training.

|                 |                    |                   |            |
|-----------------|--------------------|-------------------|------------|
|                 | Initial success(%) | Final accuracy(%) | $`\Delta`$ |
| Prolog FT       | 98.7               | 85.14             | $`-13.6`$  |
| Cocktail FT     | 90.7               | 85.52             | $`-5.2`$   |
| $`\Delta`$ (KB) | $`-8.0`$           | +0.38             | —          |

TABLE V: Effect of execution-guided repair on Qwen-32B performance.

Table [V](#S4.T5 "TABLE V ‣ IV-G Ablation Studies ‣ IV Experiments ‣ NeuroProlog: Multi-Task Fine-Tuning for Neurosymbolic Mathematical Reasoning via the Cocktail Effect")
compares initial generation performance with final accuracy after
execution-guided repair for Qwen-32B. The results show that the Cocktail
configuration exhibits a smaller gap between initial and final
performance than Prolog FT. This comparison characterizes the
interaction between generation quality and subsequent repair, but does
not establish a causal effect of KB supervision on repair.

## V Conclusion

We presented NeuroProlog, a neurosymbolic framework that combines
multi-task symbolic supervision with execution-guided program repair for
mathematical reasoning. The combined KB+SOLVE training improves GSM8K
accuracy over single-task Prolog fine-tuning for the evaluated models,
with gains of up to 5.54%, while MATH-500 results indicate
generalization to unseen problems. Error analysis reveals
scale-associated differences in repair behavior, with larger models
showing greater improvements in handling semantic errors. These results
demonstrate the potential of combining symbolic knowledge and execution
feedback for improving LLM-based mathematical reasoning.

Limitations and future work include scaling the KB to 1000+ entries for
advanced mathematics, comparative studies across SMT solvers and Lean,
controlled scaling experiments (1B–70B), and evaluation on MATH and
TheoremQA benchmarks.
````
